segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For freedom Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not let yourselves be held again in a yoke of slavery.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Look: I, Paul, tell you that if you have yourselves circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I testify again to every man who has himself circumcised that he is obligated to keep the whole law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You have been severed from Christ, you who are trying to be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For through the Spirit, by faith, we eagerly await the hope of righteousness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything; what counts is faith working through love.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You were running well. Who cut in on you and kept you from being persuaded by the truth?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That persuasion does not come from the one who calls you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A little leaven leavens the whole batch of dough.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am persuaded about you in the Lord that you will think no differently. But the one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As for me, brothers and sisters, if I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the stumbling block of the cross has been done away with.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I wish those who are unsettling you would go on and castrate themselves!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you were called to freedom, brothers and sisters. Only do not let that freedom become an opening for the flesh, but through love be slaves to one another.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the whole law is fulfilled in a single saying:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What I mean is this: walk by the Spirit, and you will certainly not carry out the desire of the flesh.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the flesh desires what is against the Spirit, and the Spirit what is against the flesh; for these are opposed to each other, so that you do not do whatever you want.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the works of the flesh are plain to see: sexual immorality, impurity, debauchery,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: idolatry, sorcery, hostilities, strife, jealousy, outbursts of rage, selfish rivalries, dissensions, factions,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: envy, drunkenness, carousing, and things like these. I tell you in advance, as I told you before, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: gentleness, self-control. Against such things there is no law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another.

notes.traditional: Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free
notes.note: The Greek is a bare dative, 'to/for/with freedom'. Most scholars take it as purpose ('for freedom'), but it can also be read as means ('with freedom Christ set us free'). Later manuscripts smooth the wording and join it to the command that follows, which is the form the King James Version translates.

'Justified' here and 'righteousness' in verse 5 translate one Greek word-family, where English has two (just/righteous, justify/righteousness). The verb means to declare or put someone in the right. The present tense describes an attempt in progress, hence 'trying to be justified'.

The phrase can mean 'the righteousness we hope for', that is, the final verdict still awaited. It can also mean 'what righteousness leads us to hope for'. Most interpreters prefer the first; the translation keeps the Greek's open wording.

The verb means to be persuaded and so to comply, and most translations render it 'obey' here. 'Persuaded' is used to keep Paul's wordplay visible: the same root returns in 'that persuasion' (verse 8) and 'I am persuaded' (verse 10). The sense of yielding to the truth, not merely agreeing with it, is included.

The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women as siblings, and Paul is writing to whole congregations. 'Brothers' alone now sounds male-only in English. Several modern translations render it the same way.

notes.traditional: were even cut off (KJV); emasculate themselves
notes.note: The verb means 'cut off', and in this form it was used of castration. Paul's bitter joke is that those pressing circumcision should let the knife go further. Older English versions softened this to 'cut off', as if he meant exclusion from the community; almost all modern scholars read it as castration.

From here on, 'flesh' in this chapter is not the physical body as such. It is human nature left to itself, self-directed and opposed to God's Spirit. The list in verses 19–21 shows this, since most of its items (strife, jealousy, factions) are not bodily sins. Some translations paraphrase it as 'sinful nature'; the traditional word is kept because the Greek is the same word used of circumcised flesh earlier in the letter.

The verb is the ordinary word for serving as a slave, from the same root as 'slavery' in verse 1. Most translations soften it to 'serve'. The paradox is deliberate: those freed from the yoke of slavery are to enslave themselves to each other through love.

notes.phrase: you will certainly not carry out
notes.note: The Greek is an emphatic negative that normally expresses a strong denial about the future, so it is translated here as a promise. A few translations take it as a second command ('and do not gratify'). The grammar favours the promise, and most scholars read it that way.

notes.phrase: so that you do not do whatever you want
notes.traditional: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would
notes.note: The clause can express result (the conflict means you do not do what you want) or purpose (each side aims to block what you want). It is also disputed what is frustrated: the good the person wishes to do, the desires of the flesh, or both. The translation leaves this as open as the Greek does.

The Greek word covers both 'faith' (trust) and 'faithfulness' (reliability). In a list of qualities shown toward other people, such as patience, kindness and goodness, most modern scholars and translations take it as faithfulness. Older versions have 'faith'.

The traditional 'meekness' now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a gentle, humble, unassertive manner toward others. 'Gentleness' or 'humility' is the usual rendering in modern translations.

candidates.reason: Paul's ethical use (human nature opposed to the Spirit) is rendered 'flesh', 'sinful nature' or 'human nature' by different translations and needs one policy across the letters.
The plural address to mixed congregations recurs in every letter, and 'brothers' versus 'brothers and sisters' must be consistent.
It recurs across the Gospels and letters and is variously rendered 'offense', 'stumbling block', 'obstacle' or 'trap'.
It is frequent in vice lists and in the divorce sayings, where 'fornication', 'sexual immorality' and 'unchastity' compete and its scope is disputed.
The Semitic idiom for conduct recurs throughout Paul and John, and translators split between 'walk' and 'live'; here it also needs to stay distinct from ζάω and στοιχέω in verse 25.
